title: Fair Ten-Sided Die From Seven-Sided Rolls
statement:
You only own a fair 7-sided die (faces 1 to 7) and need fair rolls of a 10-sided die (faces 1 to 10, each with probability exactly 1/10).

In an interview this comes as "implement rand10() using only rand7()". So that tests are repeatable, here the 7-sided rolls are given up front as an array rolls, and everyone uses the same rejection rule:

  • Take the rolls two at a time, in order: (a, b). Read the pair as a cell c = (a − 1) · 7 + b, a number from 1 to 49, each equally likely.
  • If c ≤ 40, output ((c − 1) mod 10) + 1.
  • If c > 40, throw the pair away and output nothing for it.

A single leftover roll at the end is ignored. Return the list of 10-sided results in order. The real work is understanding why this rule is fair and why simpler rules are not; the explanation covers that.

examples.why: (3, 4) is cell 18, which gives 8. (7, 1) is cell 43, above 40, so it is thrown away. The lone 2 at the end is ignored.
Cell 1 gives 1, cell 40 gives 10, and cell 41 is rejected.
Cell 10 gives 10 and cell 11 wraps around to 1: the labels repeat every 10 cells.

hints: One roll has 7 outcomes and 10 does not divide 7. How many equally likely outcomes do two rolls give?
Two rolls give 49 equally likely cells. 49 is not a multiple of 10 either, but 40 is. What do you do with the other 9 cells?
Keep cells 1 to 40, four per label, and reroll on 41 to 49. Each label then has probability 4/40 = 1/10 among accepted pairs.

explain.intuition:
Fairness needs a set of equally likely outcomes whose count is a multiple of 10. One roll gives 7 outcomes, which does not work. Two rolls, read as a row a and a column b of a 7 × 7 board, give 49 equally likely cells. Throw away the 9 extra cells and keep 40: each label 1 to 10 owns exactly 4 of them, so once a pair is accepted every label has probability 1/10. Rejected pairs do not bias anything, because you simply try again with fresh rolls. That is rejection sampling.

The tempting shortcuts are all unfair. a + b is not uniform (7 is far more common than 2). Using c mod 10 on all 49 cells gives labels 1 to 9 five cells each and label 10 only four. On average a pair is accepted with probability 40/49, so one 10-sided roll costs about 2 · 49/40 ≈ 2.45 seven-sided rolls.
steps: Walk through rolls two at a time while a full pair remains.
If c ≤ 40, push ((c − 1) mod 10) + 1; otherwise push nothing.
Return the outputs. In the interview version, wrap the loop in rand10() and repeat until a pair is accepted.
pitfalls: Using a + b or a · b: the results are not equally likely.
Taking c mod 10 over all 49 cells, which makes 10 rarer than the other labels.
Computing the cell as a · 7 + b without subtracting 1, which shifts the range to 8 … 56 and breaks the 40-cell cut.

solutions.title: Walk the pairs
solutions.idea: Turn each pair into a cell from 1 to 49, keep cells up to 40 and label them mod 10.

solutions.title: Interview shape: rand10 built on rand7
solutions.idea: Wrap the array in a rand7() function and write rand10() exactly as you would with a real random source, looping until a pair is accepted.

followups: A rejected cell from 41 to 49 is itself a uniform number from 1 to 9. How can you reuse it instead of throwing it away, and how many rolls does that save on average?
Build a fair 7-sided die from a fair 10-sided die. Do you still need rejection?
